item_name: CONSTANT AIRSPEED - CONSTANT RATE CLIMBS / DESCENTS AND VERTICAL "S"

error_modes.label: Airspeed control in constant airspeed climb / descent

texts.0: SP, due to pitch inputs made without reference to the airspeed trend, did not hold the briefed speed once the power was set for the constant airspeed climb. Airspeed diverged past 20 knots from the target and the divergence continued to build with each input. The IP intervened on the controls to reset the pitch attitude before the profile could be continued.
texts.1: SP, due to trimming after each deviation instead of first establishing the correct pitch attitude, allowed the airspeed in the constant airspeed climb and descent to reach the 20 knot limit. The excursion was corrected only after repeated verbal indications from the IP, and the return to the briefed speed was slow.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial pitch attitude set slightly low for the power applied, allowed the airspeed to move between 10 and 20 knots off the briefed value. SP identified the trend on the airspeed indicator and re-established the briefed speed in good time, without any intervention by the IP.
texts.3: SP set pitch attitude and power for the briefed value and held the constant airspeed climb and descent within 10 knots throughout. Corrections were small, applied early against the airspeed trend, and each one was trimmed off before the next segment.
texts.4: SP established the climb and descent attitude immediately and held the briefed airspeed with deviations barely readable on the indicator. Pitch and power were coordinated so that no correction greater than a few knots was ever required.
texts.marginal: SP held the constant airspeed climb and descent inside standards, but the deviations sat consistently toward the fast side of the band and were corrected only after they had developed. The tendency is to chase the indicator rather than to fix the attitude and work the trend. SP is expected to set attitude, trim, and then correct against the trend on the following sorties.

texts_at.0: With the IP calling for the pitch attitude to be established first and demonstrating the trim that follows, SP trimmed on the sequence given. The order of establishing pitch before trimming has not yet been learned, so trim is still applied after each deviation rather than the correct attitude being set first. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin establishing the correct pitch attitude first without the return being prompted.
texts_at.1: SP returned to the briefed speed only after repeated verbal indications from the IP, with the excursion reaching about 20 knots, at the limit of the standard, because trim had been applied after each deviation instead of the correct pitch attitude being established first. The return was slow once the indications had been given. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to establish the correct pitch attitude first without needing the return prompted.

This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to set the initial pitch attitude correctly for the power applied rather than correcting it afterward.
texts_at.3: SP set pitch attitude and power for the briefed value and held the constant airspeed climb and descent within 10 knots throughout, with corrections small, applied early against the airspeed trend and each one trimmed off before the next segment. One segment let the airspeed edge toward the fast side before the correction caught it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to bring every segment to the same tightness as the best one.

error_modes.label: Altitude capture and level-off from constant airspeed climb / descent

texts.0: SP, due to an interrupted instrument cross-check while attention remained on the airspeed indicator, did not begin the level-off at a lead point related to the rate of climb. The overshoot of the assigned altitude exceeded 300 feet and continued to increase. The IP took the controls to arrest the climb and re-establish level flight.
texts.1: SP, due to absent cross-check of altitude against vertical velocity while approaching the assigned level, started the level-off late. The excursion reached the 300 foot limit and the aircraft was returned to the assigned altitude only after the IP had called the deviation twice.
texts.2: SP, due to a lead point taken from habit rather than from the indicated rate, passed the assigned altitude by more than 150 feet. The deviation was picked up on the altimeter during the scan and flown back inside 150 feet promptly, without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP cross-checked altitude against vertical velocity, led the level-off appropriately for the rate being flown, and captured the assigned altitude within 150 feet. Power was reset for level flight as the attitude was changed, so the airspeed stayed under control through the transition.
texts.4: SP anticipated every level-off and stopped the altimeter on the assigned value with virtually no overshoot. Attitude, power and trim were applied as one coordinated sequence and the aircraft settled directly into level flight.
texts.marginal: SP captured the assigned altitudes inside standards, but each level-off showed the same overshoot in the same direction before the correction. The lead point is applied without reference to the actual rate of climb or descent. SP is expected to scale the lead to the indicated vertical velocity and remove the recurring overshoot.

texts_at.0: With the IP calling the deviation as the assigned level was approached, SP began the level-off on the call given. The cross-check of altitude against vertical velocity approaching a level has not yet been learned, so the level-off is still started late until the IP calls the deviation. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin keeping altitude in the cross-check on approach without the deviation being called.

One level-off used a lead a shade smaller than the rate called for. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to scale every lead point as precisely as the best one.

error_modes.label: Heading and bank control in constant airspeed climb / descent

texts.0: SP, due to rudder pressure applied with the power change and never trimmed out, did not keep the wings level during the constant airspeed climb. Heading drifted more than 10 degrees from the assigned value and bank exceeded 10 degrees while the SP worked the airspeed. The IP intervened to level the aircraft and re-establish the assigned heading.
texts.1: SP, due to a scan that excluded the heading indicator once the climb was established, allowed the heading to reach 10 degrees off the assigned value with bank at the 10 degree limit. The wings were levelled and the heading regained only after verbal direction from the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to uncompensated yaw with the power adjustment, allowed the heading to move between 5 and 10 degrees off the assigned value with a corresponding small bank. SP saw the drift on the attitude indicator and heading indicator and corrected back inside 5 degrees without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP kept the wings level within 5 degrees of bank and held the assigned heading within 5 degrees throughout the climbs and descents. Rudder was applied with each power change so the aircraft remained in balance and no heading correction was needed at the level-off.
texts.4: SP held the assigned heading with deviations that were not perceptible on the indicator and kept the wings level throughout. Power changes were made with matching rudder so that neither heading nor bank was disturbed at entry or at level-off.
texts.marginal: SP kept heading and bank inside standards, but the aircraft drifted consistently in one direction whenever attention moved to airspeed. Balance is not maintained during power changes. SP is expected to trim rudder with each power adjustment so heading is held without repeated corrections.

texts_at.0: With the IP directing the wings level and the heading correction once the climb was established, SP corrected on the direction given. The habit of keeping the heading indicator in the scan once a climb is established has not yet been built, so the scan is still excluding it until the IP directs a correction. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to begin keeping the heading indicator in the scan through the climb without it being directed.

error_modes.label: Vertical velocity control in constant rate climb / descent

texts.0: SP, due to power changes made in large steps without allowing the vertical velocity indicator to settle, did not stabilize the briefed rate of climb. The indicated rate varied by more than 300 feet per minute from the target and the excursions grew with each input. The IP intervened on the controls to set pitch and power for the briefed rate.
texts.1: SP, due to chasing the vertical velocity needle with pitch alone, allowed the rate to reach 300 feet per minute from the briefed value. The rate was recovered only after the IP called for the power adjustment, and stabilization on the briefed value was slow.
texts.2: SP, due to a power setting slightly low for the briefed rate at entry, allowed the descent rate to sit between 150 and 300 feet per minute off target. SP recognized the trend, adjusted power and pitch together and re-established the briefed rate in good time without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP set pitch and power together at entry and held the briefed rate within 150 feet per minute in both the climb and the descent. Corrections were small and made against the needle trend rather than against the instantaneous indication.
texts.4: SP stabilized the briefed rate immediately after entry and held it with deviations that were hardly discernible on the vertical velocity indicator. Rate and airspeed were controlled together so that no large correction was required at any stage.
texts.marginal: SP held the briefed rates inside standards, but the needle was worked continuously with small pitch inputs instead of being settled with a correct power setting. Rate stability degraded each time attention moved to another instrument. SP is expected to set power for the rate, trim, and then hold it with minimum control input.

texts_at.0: With the IP calling for the power adjustment to recover the briefed rate, SP adjusted power on the call given. The setting of pitch and power together for a briefed rate has not yet been learned, so the vertical velocity needle is still chased with pitch alone until the IP calls for a power adjustment. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to begin setting pitch and power together without them being set by the IP.

SP is expected to set pitch and power together without needing them set by the IP.

texts_at.3: SP set pitch and power together at entry and held the briefed rate within 150 feet per minute in both the climb and the descent, with corrections small and made against the needle trend rather than the instantaneous indication. error_modes.label: Simultaneous control of rate and airspeed

texts.0: SP, due to task sequencing that concentrated all cockpit workload on one parameter at a time, did not control rate and airspeed as a pair. Every correction applied to the vertical velocity produced an airspeed excursion beyond 20 knots, and neither parameter was recovered. The IP intervened to re-establish the aircraft on the briefed profile.
texts.1: SP, due to inadequate workload management once the constant rate descent was established, worked the vertical velocity to the exclusion of the airspeed. Airspeed reached the 20 knot limit while the rate was being held, and both parameters were restored only after successive verbal directions from the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to workload management that addressed the two parameters in turn rather than together, allowed the airspeed to move beyond 10 knots while re-establishing the briefed rate. SP recognized the coupling, set power for the rate and attitude for the speed, and returned both inside limits without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP controlled pitch and power as a pair, holding the briefed rate within 150 feet per minute and the airspeed within 10 knots at the same time. Each correction was made with its effect on the other parameter anticipated.
texts.4: SP flew rate and airspeed as one problem, with power set for the rate and attitude for the speed, and both remained essentially on target throughout the climbs and descents. Continuous use of trim meant no sustained control pressure was carried at any point.
texts.marginal: SP kept both rate and airspeed inside standards, but attention alternated between them so that improving one briefly degraded the other. Control of pitch and power remains sequential rather than combined. SP is expected to anticipate the coupling between the two parameters and remove the alternating trend.

texts_at.0: With the IP giving successive verbal directions to restore rate and then airspeed, SP corrected each parameter on the direction given. Workload management between vertical velocity and airspeed has not yet been learned, so one parameter is still worked to the exclusion of the other until the IP directs both restored. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to begin working rate and airspeed together without both needing to be restored by direction.

The aircraft passed more than 300 feet below the assigned level and the descent continued unchecked. The IP intervened on the controls to recover the altitude.
texts.1: SP, due to a level-off initiated on reaching the altitude rather than before it, went through the assigned level by the full 300 feet permitted. The altitude was regained only after the IP directed the correction, and the recovery was late in relation to the rate flown.
texts.2: SP, due to a lead point that did not account for the higher rate being flown, passed the assigned altitude by more than 150 feet. The deviation was seen on the altimeter and corrected back inside 150 feet promptly and without prompting from the IP.
texts.3: SP scaled the lead point to the rate being flown and levelled off within 150 feet of the assigned altitude. Power was reset for level flight as the pitch was changed, so the airspeed did not deviate through the transition.
texts.4: SP arrested every constant rate climb and descent on the assigned altitude with no discernible overshoot. Lead, pitch change, power reset and trim were applied as one smooth and continuous sequence.

The lead point is not being adjusted for the rate flown. SP is expected to derive the lead from the indicated rate so that the level-off no longer needs a recovery.

error_modes.label: Reversal point control in the Vertical S

texts.0: SP, due to a reversal started without the lead needed to stop the climb on the reference altitude, did not change from climb to descent at the briefed point of the Vertical S. Altitude at the reversal was more than 300 feet from the assigned value and the briefed rate was not re-established in the opposite direction. The IP intervened on the controls to recover the maneuver.
texts.1: SP, due to a reversal flown by altimeter indication alone with no anticipation of the rate, reached the 300 foot limit at the reversal point of the Vertical S maneuver. The rate in the new direction was set only after the IP called for it, and the maneuver continued displaced from the reference altitude.
texts.2: SP, due to a lead applied late at the top of the climb segment, went through the reference altitude of the Vertical S by more than 150 feet before the descent was established. SP identified the excursion and set the briefed rate in the new direction in good time, without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP anticipated each reversal of the Vertical S, arrested the vertical velocity within 150 feet of the reference altitude and established the briefed rate in the opposite direction immediately. Pitch and power were changed together so that the airspeed remained on the briefed value through the reversal.
texts.4: SP reversed the Vertical S precisely on the reference altitude with the new rate established immediately and no perceptible pause in the vertical velocity. The transitions were flown so smoothly that airspeed and heading were unaffected.
texts.marginal: SP flew the Vertical S reversals inside standards, but each one required a visible correction back toward the reference altitude before the new rate settled. The lead into the reversal is applied too late for the rate being flown. SP is expected to anticipate the reversal so that the altitude and the new rate are achieved together.

error_modes.label: Bank control during turning segments of the Vertical S

texts.0: SP, due to bank being varied to correct vertical velocity during the Vertical S, did not hold the briefed angle of bank in the turning segments. Bank exceeded 10 degrees from the briefed value and the resulting heading error grew beyond 10 degrees. The IP intervened to re-establish the briefed bank and the turn.
texts.1: SP, due to attention held on the vertical velocity indicator through the turn, allowed the bank in the Vertical S to reach 10 degrees from the briefed angle with the rollout heading equally displaced. The bank was reset only after the IP called the deviation.
texts.2: SP, due to the pitch change at the reversal being made without holding the bank, allowed the angle of bank to vary between 5 and 10 degrees from the briefed value. SP corrected the bank on the attitude indicator and completed the turn on the briefed heading without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP held the briefed angle of bank within 5 degrees throughout the turning segments of the Vertical S and rolled out within 5 degrees of the briefed heading. Bank was maintained independently of the pitch and power changes at each reversal.
texts.4: SP held the briefed bank with deviations that were not readable on the attitude indicator and rolled out exactly on the briefed headings. The reversals were flown without any disturbance to the turn.

texts.1: SP, due to an over-controlled aircraft (AE104) at each correction, made large and abrupt attitude changes to recover flight parameters. Deviations reached the limits of the allowed band and the aircraft was steadied only after the IP called for smaller and smoother inputs.
texts.2: SP, due to control inputs made in steps rather than continuously, induced attitude changes larger than the correction required and deviations grew beyond the code 3 band. texts.3: SP controlled the aircraft smoothly and continuously, with no extreme or repeated attitude changes made to correct flight parameter deviations. Each correction was sized to the deviation and trimmed off, and all parameters stayed within the code 3 band.
texts.4: SP handled the aircraft smoothly throughout, with corrections so small and so well anticipated that no attitude change was perceptible on the instruments. Trim was used continuously and the aircraft was never displaced by a correction.

texts_at.0: With the IP calling for smaller and smoother inputs at each correction, SP applied the sizing called for. texts_above.3: SP controlled the aircraft smoothly and continuously on the whole sortie, with no extreme or repeated attitude changes made to correct flight parameter deviations, sizing each correction to the deviation and trimming it off so all parameters stayed within the code 3 band. texts.0: SP, due to starting the Vertical S without the aircraft completely trimmed hands-off for level flight at 150 knots, did not have a stable datum from which to set the target pitch and power. texts.2: SP, due to accepting a level flight trim state that was close but not hands-off before the entry, allowed the climb segment of the Vertical S to sit between 150 and 300 feet per minute off the briefed rate. texts.4: SP established the aircraft completely trimmed hands-off at 150 knots before entry, so the target pitch and power were set from a stable datum with no control force to hold. Rate and altitude deviations through the whole Vertical S were hardly discernible on the instruments.
texts.marginal: SP flew the Vertical S inside standards, but the entry was made with the aircraft not yet trimmed hands-off, so every segment began with a stick force that had to be trimmed out in the climb. The deviations sit toward the limit at the first reversal and settle only later in the maneuver. SP is expected to complete the level flight trim at 150 knots before the entry so the profile starts from a stable datum.

texts_at.0: With the IP calling for the aircraft to be trimmed hands-off before entry, SP trimmed on the call given. texts_at.3: SP trimmed the aircraft hands-off for level flight at 150 knots before starting the Vertical S, then set power and pitch attitude to the target values together, holding the briefed rate within 150 feet per minute and the reference altitudes within 150 feet throughout the maneuver. error_modes.label: Trim not reset for the power change in the constant airspeed climb / descent
error_modes.source: technique:7.10 CONSTANT AIRSPEED CLIMBS AND DESCENTS

texts.0: SP, due to treating the constant airspeed climb as a constant trim condition, did not trim for the power change on the assumption that no trim was required while the airspeed stayed the same. The held stick force was released progressively during the cross-check and the airspeed diverged past 20 knots from the briefed value. The IP intervened on the controls to retrim and re-establish the profile.

SP identified the drift, completed the trim and restored the briefed airspeed in good time without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP trimmed the aircraft for each power change even though the airspeed was to remain constant, and held the briefed airspeed within 10 knots through both the climb and the descent. No control force was carried while the cross-check moved between instruments.
texts.4: SP trimmed immediately after every power change so the aircraft flew the constant airspeed climb and descent hands-off at the briefed value. Airspeed deviations were barely perceptible on the indicator throughout.
texts.marginal: SP held the constant airspeed climb and descent inside standards, but trim was applied late after each power change and the airspeed drifted while the stick force was still being held. The link between power change and trim change is not yet automatic. SP is expected to trim as part of every power change so the airspeed no longer wanders during the cross-check.

texts_at.3: SP trimmed the aircraft for each power change even though the airspeed was to remain constant, holding the briefed airspeed within 10 knots through both the climb and the descent with no control force carried while the cross-check moved between instruments. error_modes.label: Speed brake used without allowing for the larger pitch change required
error_modes.source: technique:7.10 CONSTANT AIRSPEED CLIMBS AND DESCENTS

texts.4: SP anticipated the pitch change needed for the speed brake at both extension and retraction, so the briefed airspeed was held with deviations that were hardly discernible. The descent rate remained steady through each configuration change.

error_modes.label: Entry pitch and power not set from known values before fine tuning the rate
error_modes.source: technique:7.11 CONSTANT RATE CLIMBS AND DESCENTS

texts.0: SP, due to entering the constant rate descent without the known pitch and power settings for the briefed rate and without applying the sixty-to-one relationship to derive the pitch change, searched for the attitude with successive guesses. The indicated rate never stabilized and stayed more than 300 feet per minute from the briefed value with the airspeed diverging with it. The IP intervened on the controls to set the known pitch and power for the maneuver.

The pitch change applied was consistent with the rate and true airspeed being flown.
texts.4: SP entered on the known pitch and power settings so the briefed rate was achieved almost immediately, and the fine tuning after stabilization amounted to a barely perceptible pitch change. Rate and airspeed remained steady for the whole segment.

texts_at.2: SP waited for the vertical speed to stabilize, then applied the small pitch change required and settled on the briefed rate in good time without IP intervention, after an entry attitude estimated rather than derived for the briefed rate let the indicated rate sit about 200 feet per minute off target. texts_at.3: SP set the known pitch and power settings at entry, waited for the vertical speed to stabilize and only then fine tuned, holding the briefed rate within 150 feet per minute and the airspeed within 10 knots, with the pitch change applied consistent with the rate and true airspeed being flown. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good use of known entry pitch and power settings.
texts_above.3: SP set the known pitch and power settings at entry on every segment of the sortie, waiting for the vertical speed to stabilize and only then fine tuning, holding the briefed rate within 150 feet per minute and the airspeed within 10 knots. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined use of known entry pitch and power settings.

error_modes.label: Airspeed corrections not scaled through small vertical speed changes
error_modes.source: technique:7.10 CONSTANT AIRSPEED CLIMBS AND DESCENTS

texts.0: SP, due to correcting a small airspeed error with a large pitch input instead of adjusting the vertical speed by about 100 feet per minute for each 2 knots to be regained, drove the aircraft between opposite excursions. The rate departed the briefed value by more than 300 feet per minute and the airspeed error was not removed. The IP intervened on the controls to steady the attitude and re-establish the profile.
texts.1: SP, due to airspeed corrections applied as large vertical speed changes, allowed the rate in the constant airspeed climb to reach the 300 feet per minute limit while chasing a few knots of error. The oscillation stopped only after the IP called for smaller pitch corrections.
texts.2: SP, due to a correction sized for a larger error than the one indicated, allowed the vertical speed to move between 150 and 300 feet per minute from the briefed value while the airspeed was regained. SP recognized the oversized correction, reduced the pitch input and restored both parameters in good time without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP regained small airspeed errors with correspondingly small vertical speed changes, of the order of 100 feet per minute for 2 knots, and kept the airspeed within 10 knots and the rate within 150 feet per minute. No correction had to be taken out again.
texts.4: SP corrected the few knots of airspeed error with pitch changes so small that the vertical speed excursion was hardly discernible on the indicator. Airspeed and rate were both held essentially on the briefed values throughout.
texts.marginal: SP kept airspeed and rate inside standards, but every small airspeed error was answered with a vertical speed change far larger than the error required, producing a second deviation to correct. The scaling between airspeed error and pitch correction is not yet established. SP is expected to size the vertical speed change to the knots to be regained so one correction settles the parameter.

texts_at.0: With the IP calling for smaller pitch corrections to stop the oscillation, SP applied the sizing called for. The scaling of a vertical speed change to a small airspeed error has not yet been learned, so a few knots of error are still chased with a large rate change until the IP calls for a smaller correction. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin scaling the vertical speed change to the airspeed error without a smaller correction being called.
texts_at.1: SP had the oscillation stopped only after the IP called for smaller pitch corrections, with the rate reaching the 300 feet per minute limit while chasing a few knots of error, because airspeed corrections had been applied as large vertical speed changes. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to scale the vertical speed change to the airspeed error without needing the correction called.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the oversized correction, reduced the pitch input and restored both parameters in good time without IP intervention, after a correction sized for a larger error than indicated let the vertical speed move about 250 feet per minute from the briefed value while airspeed was regained. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to size the first correction to the actual error rather than reducing it afterward.
texts_at.3: SP regained small airspeed errors with correspondingly small vertical speed changes, of the order of 100 feet per minute for 2 knots. Every correction was taken out as the parameter came back, so airspeed held within 10 knots and the rate within 150 feet per minute throughout. One correction was a shade larger than the error called for. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to scale every correction as precisely as the tightest one.

texts_above.1: SP scaled the vertical speed change to the airspeed error, containing the rate to the 300 feet per minute limit. A verbal call from the IP came before the correction. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized an oversized correction and reduced the pitch input, restoring both parameters in good time without IP intervention, holding the vertical speed deviation between 150 and 300 feet per minute after a correction sized for a larger error than indicated. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady scaling of airspeed corrections to the vertical-speed change.
texts_above.3: SP regained every small airspeed error with a correspondingly small vertical speed change, of the order of 100 feet per minute for 2 knots, keeping airspeed within 10 knots and the rate within 150 feet per minute on the whole sortie with no correction ever needing to be taken back out. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate scaling of airspeed corrections to the vertical-speed change.
texts_above.4: SP corrected the few knots of airspeed error with pitch changes so small that the vertical speed excursion was hardly discernible on the indicator, with airspeed and rate both held essentially on the briefed values throughout. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional scaling of airspeed corrections to the vertical-speed change.

error_modes.label: Descent pitch and torque combination not set for the briefed airspeed
error_modes.source: technique:7.10 CONSTANT AIRSPEED CLIMBS AND DESCENTS

texts.0: SP, due to entering the constant airspeed descent with a nose-low attitude and a torque setting that did not form a valid combination for the briefed airspeed, produced an attitude and power pairing that could not hold 200 knots. Airspeed diverged past 20 knots from the briefed value and continued to build as the descent progressed. The IP intervened on the controls to set a matched pitch and torque combination.
texts.1: SP, due to setting the nose-low attitude first and adjusting torque only afterwards, allowed the airspeed in the constant airspeed descent to reach the 20 knot limit. The matched pitch and torque combination was established only after verbal indications from the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to a torque setting slightly high for the nose-low attitude selected, allowed the descent airspeed to sit between 10 and 20 knots above the briefed value. SP identified the mismatch, reduced torque to suit the attitude being flown and regained the briefed airspeed in good time without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP set a pitch and torque combination consistent with the briefed descent airspeed and held it within 10 knots throughout the segment. The rate produced by the combination was steady and required no repeated adjustment.
texts.4: SP selected the nose-low attitude and matching torque together at entry, so the briefed descent airspeed was achieved at once and held with deviations that were hardly discernible. No further power adjustment was needed during the descent.
texts.marginal: SP held the descent airspeed inside standards, but the attitude and torque were selected independently and then reconciled by trial, so the airspeed sat toward the fast side of the band for most of the segment. The pitch and power pairing for the briefed airspeed is not yet known from memory. SP is expected to set a matched attitude and torque combination at entry rather than arriving at it by successive corrections.

texts_at.0: With the IP giving verbal indications to match torque to the nose-low attitude, SP adjusted torque on the indications given. The combination of pitch and torque for a briefed descent airspeed has not yet been learned, so torque is still adjusted only after the attitude is set rather than together with it. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin selecting the pitch and torque combination together without it being directed.
texts_at.1: SP had the pitch and torque combination set only after verbal indications from the IP, with airspeed reaching the 20 knot limit, because the nose-low attitude had been set first and torque adjusted only afterward. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to select the pitch and torque combination together without needing it directed.
texts_at.2: SP identified the mismatch, reduced torque to suit the attitude being flown and regained the briefed airspeed in good time without IP intervention, after a torque setting slightly high for the nose-low attitude selected let the descent airspeed sit about 15 knots above the briefed value. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to select the matched torque for the attitude at entry rather than correct it afterward.
texts_at.3: SP set a pitch and torque combination consistent with the briefed descent airspeed and held it within 10 knots throughout the segment, with the rate produced by the combination steady and needing no repeated adjustment. One descent needed the torque trimmed a beat after the attitude was set. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to bring every descent to the same match as the cleanest one.

texts_above.1: SP set pitch and torque together for the constant airspeed descent, containing airspeed to the 20 knot limit. SP corrected after a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP identified a mismatch and reduced torque to suit the attitude being flown, regaining the briefed airspeed in good time without IP intervention, holding the deviation between 10 and 20 knots after a torque setting slightly high for the nose-low attitude selected. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound pitch and torque combination for the descent airspeed.
texts_above.3: SP set a pitch and torque combination consistent with the briefed descent airspeed on every segment of the sortie, holding it within 10 knots throughout with the rate produced by the combination steady and needing no repeated adjustment. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed pitch and torque combination for the descent airspeed.
texts_above.4: SP selected the nose-low attitude and matching torque together at entry, so the briefed descent airspeed was achieved at once and held with deviations hardly discernible, with no further power adjustment ever needed during the descent. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior pitch and torque combination for the descent airspeed.

error_modes.label: Nose not lowered after the climb airspeed is reached

texts.0: SP, due to holding the entry pitch attitude after the desired climb airspeed had been reached, did not lower the nose to keep the airspeed constant as the altitude increased. Airspeed decayed more than 20 knots below the briefed value as performance fell off with altitude and the climb could not be continued as briefed. The IP intervened on the controls to lower the nose and restore the climb airspeed.
texts.1: SP, due to leaving the pitch attitude unchanged while the aircraft climbed, allowed the constant airspeed climb to reach the 20 knot limit on the slow side. The nose was lowered only after repeated verbal indications from the IP and the briefed airspeed was slow to return.
texts.2: SP, due to lowering the nose later than the airspeed trend required as altitude increased, allowed the climb airspeed to sit between 10 and 20 knots below the briefed value. SP recognized the decay, adjusted the pitch attitude and re-established the briefed airspeed in good time without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP set the pitch attitude to achieve the desired climb airspeed and then lowered the nose progressively as the altitude increased, keeping the airspeed within 10 knots throughout the climb. The attitude changes were small and each one was trimmed off.
texts.4: SP adjusted the pitch attitude continuously as the aircraft climbed, so the briefed climb airspeed was held with deviations that were hardly discernible on the indicator. The rate of climb changed with altitude without any airspeed excursion.
texts.marginal: SP held the climb airspeed inside standards, but the airspeed decayed toward the slow side of the band at each stage of the climb before the nose was lowered. The pitch attitude is being set once rather than adjusted continuously as altitude increases. SP is expected to lower the nose against the airspeed trend so the briefed speed is held without repeated recoveries.

texts_at.0: With the IP giving repeated verbal indications to lower the nose as the climb airspeed decayed, SP lowered the nose on the indications given. The progressive lowering of the nose as altitude increases has not yet been learned, so the pitch attitude is still left unchanged until the IP indicates the correction. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to begin lowering the nose progressively as altitude increases without it being directed.
texts_at.1: SP had the nose lowered only after repeated verbal indications from the IP, with airspeed reaching the 20 knot limit on the slow side, because the pitch attitude had been left unchanged while the aircraft climbed. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to lower the nose progressively as altitude increases without needing it directed.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the decay, adjusted the pitch attitude and re-established the briefed airspeed in good time without IP intervention, after lowering the nose later than the airspeed trend required let the climb airspeed sit about 15 knots below the briefed value. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to lower the nose on the trend rather than after the decay develops.
texts_at.3: SP set the pitch attitude to achieve the desired climb airspeed and then lowered the nose progressively as the altitude increased, keeping the airspeed within 10 knots throughout the climb with the attitude changes small and each one trimmed off. One climb let the airspeed edge toward the slow side before the correction caught it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to bring every climb to the same tightness as the best one.

texts_above.1: SP lowered the nose as the aircraft climbed, containing the constant airspeed climb to the 20 knot limit on the slow side. The IP's call came first, and the correction followed it. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized a decay and adjusted the pitch attitude, re-establishing the briefed airspeed in good time without IP intervention, holding the deviation between 10 and 20 knots after lowering the nose later than the airspeed trend required. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good progressive nose-lowering as the climb continues.
texts_above.3: SP set the pitch attitude to achieve the desired climb airspeed on every climb of the sortie and then lowered the nose progressively as altitude increased, keeping the airspeed within 10 knots throughout with the attitude changes small and each one trimmed off. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise progressive nose-lowering as the climb continues.
texts_above.4: SP adjusted the pitch attitude continuously as the aircraft climbed, so the briefed climb airspeed was held with deviations hardly discernible on the indicator and the rate of climb changed with altitude without any airspeed excursion. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding progressive nose-lowering as the climb continues.
